author: Emma Loffhagen
description:
The acclaimed American journalist, who won the nonfiction prize in 2021, is shortlisted alongside Andrea Wulf and Matthew Sweet

Former Baillie Gifford winner Patrick Radden Keefe is among the authors shortlisted for the 2026 prize, this time with his book on London’s criminal underbelly.

The six-strong shortlist spans literary biography, ancient history, true crime and international reportage, with James Baldwin, Barbara Cartland and Alexander the Great among its subjects.

Continue reading...
title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller London Falling shortlisted for Baillie Gifford prize

author: Lucy Campbell
description:
Sharon Jacks, 74, alleges hospital removed left leg instead of her right during below-the-knee amputation in 2025

An Ohio woman is suing a hospital after doctors allegedly amputated the wrong leg during a scheduled operation last year.

Sharon Jacks, 74, of Meigs county, alleged that she went to Selby general hospital in September 2025 to undergo a planned below-the-knee amputation of her right leg. Instead doctors removed her left leg during the procedure, according to the lawsuit, which was filed earlier this month in Washington county court in Marietta, where the hospital is based.

Continue reading...
title: Ohio woman sues hospital for allegedly amputating wrong leg during surgery

author: Sarah Dempster
description:
Sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Armitage shouting in a cagoule

Dr Ethan Winter is a maverick, a wildcard, a lone wolf who won’t play by the rules. “Winter!” gasps DI Lauren Bell as the muscular outsider bursts into a police interrogation room and proceeds to subject a tremulous pensioner to the full force of his waxed cagoule. “You can’t do this!” But he can do this. And he will do this. Why? Because he’s Dr Ethan Winter, dammit, one of the greatest forensic pathologists of his generation; a bearded genius whose approach to obstacles is as uncompromising as his approach to tremulous pensioners.

And yet. Dr Ethan Winter is troubled. We know this because Winter – the new six-part ITV police procedural that shares his starkly unseasonable surname – keeps cutting to scenes in which our protagonist paces silently around his fashionably underlit Bristol flat while scowling into the middle distance. Has he misplac
title: Winter review – Richard Armitage’s new cop drama is as ferociously watchable as it is daft

author: Barney Ronay
description:
What Guardiola knew at City relates to the true nature of the club and more basic things like spectacle and human nature

“Do you know the question that you are asking me? Today, do you honestly think it is my job to make this kind of question happen …” Cut to the long, painful pause. Chuck in a deep, shaming stare, eyes that have suddenly become death rays of betrayal and disgust and Pep Guardiola himself transformed from a man cheerfully toasting his own FA Cup final victory to a grizzled chief detective addressing a room full of convicted perverts.

Guardiola had the wind entirely at his back at this point, sitting in the Wembley press room an hour after Manchester City’s 6-0 defeat of Watford in May 2019. Success drowns out every other noise in football. To be good is also to be good, noble, virtuous. History is written by the domestic t
title: Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball

author: Donald McRae
description:
• Joshua reveals he is speaking to Peter Fury on training

  • Fury vows to ‘blast him out’ at London press conference

Anthony Joshua has revealed that he is in contact with Tyson Fury’s uncle Peter, in a surprise twist to the buildup between the two former world champion heavyweights who will finally meet in the ring in Cardiff in December.

Peter Fury trained Tyson when he shocked Wladimir Klitschko to win his first world heavyweight title in 2015. The uncle and nephew fell out soon afterwards, apparently over a financial dispute, and have not spoken in many years.

Continue reading...<
title: Quips, slights and a surprise twist: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury come face to face

author: Zoe Williams
description:
Be it her pioneering approach to consumer injustice or her extraordinary tackling of systemic social issues, the broadcaster was at the forefront of what television could be

  • Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86

  • Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in pictures

Esther Rantzen’s early CV reads like a chronicle of the world working as the 1960s thought it should. A smart young woman, privately educated in north London from the age of 10 (the Rantzens had previously lived in New York), then at Somerville College, Oxford, she started on the bottom rung and had exactly the right mixture of graft and luck. Having trained as a radio studio manager, she got her first TV production job as a rese
title: From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary life

author: Alexi Duggins
description:
Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner
• From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary life
• Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in pictures

Esther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86.

In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”, whose “legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her”.

Continue read
title: Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86

author: Matt Hughes
description:
• Premier League executives pushing for severe punishment

  • City maintain they are ‘innocent of the accusations’

The Premier League will face pressure from Manchester City’s rivals to push for a sanction that will result in a prolonged absence from the top flight after the club were found guilty of more than 100 charges of financial rule-breaking.

Executives at a number of Premier League clubs have told the Guardian that a points deduction that would relegate City to the Championship for a single season would be insufficient given the scale of what an independent commission described as the club’s “disguised funding scheme” and “sham commercial deals”, which enabled them to artificially inflate their income by £900m between 2009 and 2018.
title: Rival clubs feel relegating Manchester City to Championship would not be enough

author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
description:
Nationalist residents’ coalition says it will agree to proposal by Northern Ireland secretary if unionists also accept it

The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, has said an end to the Drumcree parade dispute is “tantalisingly close”, as the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition signalled it would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order did so.

Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the nationalist group, said on Wednesday afternoon he had been through the document drawn up by Bryant and his team.

Continue reading...
title: Garvaghy Road march talks ‘tantalisingly close’ to resolution, says minister

author: Matt Hughes
description:
• Club ‘a huge partner in building modern Manchester’

  • Independent Football Regulator monitoring case

Andy Burnham has said he would be “really concerned” to lose Manchester City’s owners as a result of the club being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules.

On the day that the Independent Football Regulator confirmed it has powers to investigate the suitability of the Abu Dhabi United Group to own an English club after the damning judgment of an independent commission regarding £900m of sham contracts, the prime minister praised City’s owners for their investment of billions of pounds into Manchester.

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdicts

author: Editorial
description:
Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him

Sunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, is neck and neck in the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.

Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his fathe
title: The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Empty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young people

School closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are having fewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for an ageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.

The fall has been most acute in inner London, where 90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born e
title: The Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young people | Editorial

author: Reuters
description:
• SFV withdraws support after endorsing candidacy in June

  • Swiss-born Infantino has faced calls for his resignation

The Swiss Football Association (SFV) has withdrawn its support for Gianni ⁠Infantino’s bid for another term as Fifa president, the organisation confirmed on Wednesday.

The executive committee ⁠reversed its support ⁠for Infantino, who was born in Brig, an Alpine town in Valais canton in southern Switzerland, in a meeting this week after endorsing his candidacy in June.

title: Swiss FA ‘cannot justify’ its support for Infantino’s re-election as Fifa president

From crystal balconettes on the catwalk to mankinis on the parkrun, showing off your undies seems to be all the rage

author: Ben Fisher
description:
• Wales ‘unrecognisable’ in defeat against Denmark

  • Haaland ‘exactly the same’ after Manchester City verdict

Craig Bellamy has said Wales must improve against Norway on Thursday after appearing unrecognisable in defeat against Denmark, and highlighted their next opponent’s run to the World Cup quarter-finals as proof of their talent.

Wales host Norway in Cardiff on Thursday hoping to record their first win since last November and their first since promotion to Nations League A. “This team has been on a surge,” Bellamy said of Ståle Solbakken’s side. “They are progressing and they will keep going as well – they ain’t going away, especially with the youngsters they’ve got coming through. We’ve all been waiting [for them to flourish]. But it was coming and it’s come with a bang.”

Continue reading...
title: Craig Bellamy urges Wales improvement but wary of Norway’s threat

author: Nils Pratley
description:
Ministers should introduce a properly targeted social tariff rather than tinker with the warm homes discount

  • Energy bills forecast to jump by £276 a year from January

  • What to do as prices head for £2,000 a year

After the hopeful good vibes in Liverpool, here comes a reminder of what is coming this winter: a mighty new year shock in energy bills, hitting the poorest hardest, that the government looks unprepared for.

From the quarterly price cap level of £1,723 that will apply from Thursday for an average dual-fuel household, take your pick from a range of forecasts for the first three months of 2027.
title: Government must stop dithering over energy bill support for the vulnerable | Nils Pratley

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lock

In the aftermath of Andy Burnham’s speech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September).

Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers.
title: Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Gian Lorenzo Spisso says his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evils

Reading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen.

I come from Italy, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented.
title: A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Parental influence | Public investment | Capital gains tax on property profits | A degree of success? | Oxygen of publicity

Keir Starmer reminded us often that his father was a toolmaker, a skilled occupation. In his Labour party conference speech, Andy Burnham referenced his parents, Eileen and his late father Roy. He did not mention that Roy was a telecoms engineer, also a skilled job, and one that was and is fully unionised, with decent terms and conditions. Perhaps the PM sees in that not just the past but also the future of work.
Keith Flett
Tottenham, London

• Andy Burnham’s belief that investment in public spending will save money in the longer term is a positive-sum calculus targeted at improving the quality of life. After all, if private capital can generate profit from privatised utilities and servi
title: Is this how Andy Burnham sees the future of work? | Brief letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Richard Nobbs draws attention to fundamental flaw in way pension assets are split on divorce and calls on Labour to act

Your article on the impact of the escalating cost of living on divorce settlements (Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers, 23 September) provides a timely reminder of the financial inequities facing many separating couples.

As a pensions expert, I have regularly encountered a particular imbalance in the splitting of pension assets on divorce. Although the last Labour government enabled pension savings to be taken into account in divorce settlements, there remains, 25 years on, an inherent unfairness in the way many such arrangements are implemented.
title: Unfair method of splitting pensions can add to the pain of divorce | Letters

author: Niall McVeigh
description:
⚽ Updates from the 5.45pm BST kick-off in France
⚽ Live scores | Read Moving the Goalposts | Mail Niall

ESPN and Disney+ have copped plenty of flak for their pre-game show, The Hangout, which launched before the first round of games. Judging by tonight, they’ve made things feel a little more professional (there’s no dog this time) and the guests know their stuff even if they are – gasp! – content creators. There have been technical troubles with the pitchside reporters, though.

Renée Slegers makes just two changes from the 1-0 defeat to Chelsea, with Misa Rodriguez in goal ahead of Anneke Borbe, while Lotte Wubben-Moy replaces Steph Catley in defence. Catley, like Chloe Kelly, is injured and did not travel for the game.
title: Paris FC v Arsenal: Women’s Champions League – live

author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
description:
Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi

New oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head of EDF Energy.

Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there.

Continue reading...
title: New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss

author: Adrian Chiles
description:
The Pitt is on a different level – it’s not so much like watching drama as being in one

I do like a TV doctor. I’m not talking about proper doctors who sit on studio sofas dispensing wisdom. I’ve nothing against them – why, I worked with Dr Hilary Jones on ITV and he was a very nice chap – but it’s to fictional doctors I want to entrust my care.

I’ve not always felt this way. Either the standard of fictional TV medics has improved or, more likely, I’m losing the plot. It’s a relatively recent thing. I never watched ER, for some reason, and I find Casualty to be quite entertaining without ever fantasising about being rushed into Holby City hospital for emergency treatment. As for being treated by the staff of Grey’s Anatomy, that would be fine, but the constant playing of pop songs at key moments would get on my nerves. Nurse Jackie
title: I have a new favourite medical drama – and now I want to have a nasty accident in Pittsburgh | Adrian Chiles

author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
description:
Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.

As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities

author: Zoe Wood
description:
The price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save

  • Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill forecast to jump by £276 to the equivalent of nearly £2,000 year.

It is a worrying outlook but there are practical steps you can take to mitigate the predicted price shock.

title: Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating

author: Steven Morris
description:
Their whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study finds

Naturalists have long wondered how brightly coloured butterflies manage to evade the attention of birds that make a meal of other insects.

New research from British ecologists suggests it is not simply a matter of good luck but instead a visual illusion created by their fluttering wings.

Continue reading...
title: All of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunch

author: Barry Glendenning
description:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

In the four matches they’ve sat through since their unconvincing Geopolitics World Cup win over Haiti, it must rankle among diehard conscripts of the Tartan Army that the only sporting moment they’ve been able to celebrate with genuine wild abandon remains a Wyatt Langford home run biffed out of the stadium for the Texas Rangers at Fenway Park. Away from the diamond, fairly meek surrenders by Scotland to Morocco and Brazil led to Steve Clarke’s resignation, which in turn prompted Sébastien Pocognoli to surf in on a wave of cautious fan suspicion. Following an extremely promising second-half display in his first game against Slovenia – one that obviously featured no goals, a couple of missed sitters and plenty of attacking verve from his side – the Belgian had plenty of reasons to be cheerful going into his first home game
title: Football Daily | The big story is of course … Scotland fans pining for another home run

author: Zoe Williams
description:
Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics

A number of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour party conference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission on electoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tel
title: Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak| Zoe Williams

author: Interview by Chris Broughton
description:
‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’

The late 1960s and most of the 1970s were a difficult time for New York. I’d moved there from France in 1965 with a reporter friend and a plan to start a little agency, but soon found myself working alone. It could be a dangerous city, especially at night, but I enjoyed taking pictures of everyday life around me. In 1969, I became the first foreign correspondent for the Paris-based Gamma Agency, but always insisted on working on personal projects rather than assignments.

Reading the New York Times in 1972, I would see stories about gangs in the Bronx that were killing drug-pushers who targeted young people in the area. The police would find their bodies on the kerb at the bottom of five-storey buildings they’d been thrown off. The gangs included the Savage Nomads and the Dirty Doz
title: ‘The Savage Skulls were the most dangerous gang in the Bronx’: Jean-Pierre Laffont’s best photograph

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
In a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is free

Walking into Gabriel Orozco’s show is like waking up with a headache and trying to piece together whatever the hell you did last night. Everything in the Mexican conceptualist’s exhibition is splintered, disjointed, a history you can’t make sense of.

Continue reading...
title: Explosions of colour, cold war paranoia and hyper-erotic intimacy: five free shows to see

author: Jess Cartner-Morley
description:
What you need to lift your autumn wardrobe is something flimsy, flirty and unconventional

At this time of year, my job is mostly banging on about jumpers. Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness and merino sweaters, as Keats would surely have written had he been on Substack. Cosiness is next to godliness.

I can worship at the altar of cashmere with the best of them. I can extol the virtues of a sweater in tones normally reserved for fine wines and newborn babies. But today I have a rather different proposition for your autumn wardrobe. The best fillip for your shoulder-season style is not a thick layer, but the opposite. What you need to lift your look right now is something flimsy, flirty, with an edging of lace. A sorbet-coloured lace-edged tank top that is virtually a camisole. A slinky black slip skirt with a lace hem. Something with a frill, that has the thrill of lingerie.
title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: now is the perfect time to flash some lace

author: Caramel Quin
description:
Fed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryers

• The best electric blankets and heated throws, tested by our expert

You don’t have to live in the American deep south to feel the effects of humidity. At home, just breathing makes the air more humid, let alone cooking or showering.

And when it gets too humid, it’s bad for our health as well as our homes. In fact, the two are connected: humidity lets mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.

Continue reading...
title: The best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, tested

author: John Crace
description:
Dad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lens

Is this the sketch my father would have wanted? Not something I have previously given much thought to. He died 15 years before I even started this job. But my guess is that it is. He was the loveliest of men who only ever wanted for me what I wanted for me. He was stupidly proud of even my most forgettable successes. I still see him in my dreams, cheering me on. He’d almost certainly be embarrassed, but secretly pleased, to find himself in the first paragraph.

But that’s enough about my father issues. Time now to talk about Andy Burnham’s. In his emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech on Tuesday – I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to have a politician other than Nigel Farage say exactly what he thinks and believes – Andy told us he wanted to build the country his father would have wanted. It was almost a debt of honour. Burnham was very precise. This was not
title: Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch | John Crace

author: Guardian community team
description:
Whatever the reason, we want to hear from 18-29 year olds who have never had a romantic relationship

In our age of endless dating apps, TV dating shows and couple influencers, it might seem like young people falling in love are everywhere. Yet a survey earlier this year found that a third of young adults living in the UK have actually never had a romantic partner.

According to data collected by YouGov, 33% of 18-29 year olds have never been in a relationship – so why is that? Has an increase in working from home removed opportunities to meet new people? Are young people put off by the costs involved in going on dates? Or are members of gen Z simply more content to be single than their older counterparts?

Continue reading...
title: Tell us: are you aged 18-29 and never had a romantic relationship?

author: Richard Luscombe
description:
Bear known for sitting in solitude won tournament celebrating the animals’ ability to eat large amounts of fish

A chunky ursine called Backpack has out gobbled a challenge from an outsized female nicknamed the Dancing Queen to waltz – or rather waddle – off with the Fat Bear Week title at Alaska’s Katmai national park.

Backpack, a 20-year-old quiet giant known for sitting in solitude for long periods on his rock on the Brooks river, won by barely 5,000 votes in the public tournament celebrating the brown bears’ ability to eat as many fish, Alaska rangers announced.

Continue reading...
title: Backpack edges past Dancing Queen to win the Fat Bear Week title

author: Will Unwin
description:
• I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club’

  • Former City chair Bernstein calls for directors to quit

Pep Guardiola has thrown his support behind Manchester City after the club were found guilty of all charges of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, telling fans: “We will get through this together”.

Guardiola left City in the summer after a trophy-laden decade in charge, with the period of his first two seasons part of the investigation ruled on by an independent commission. The Spaniard remains a close ally of the chief executive, Ferran Soriano, who brought him to England, the pair having previously worked together at Barcelona. City maintain their innocence and are set to appeal against the decision before Friday’s deadline.
title: ‘I am here more than ever’: Guardiola backs Manchester City owners over guilty verdicts

author: Graeme Wearden
description:
UK cements its place as fastest-growing G7 country so far this year

This morning’s upgrade to UK growth in April-June is a boost to Andy Burnham, analysts say, even though he didn’t take office until almost a month later.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, says:

“Still on a post-speech high, the upgraded figure is yet more good news for the UK’s still-new(ish) prime minister.

The highest growth in the G7 for the first half is certainly a headline and one that will help keep nervous MPs in line for a while, plus it helps take off pressure for a new election - why risk it now when things appear to be improving nicely.”

The upward revision to real
title: Economic growth in UK and US revised higher; diesel on brink of £2 a litre for first time – business live

author: Tom Phillips, Bryony Moore, Karif Wat and Boglarka Kosztolanyi
description:
Brazil will head to the polls on 4 October for the first vote in its presidential race. The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is neck-and-neck with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. There are fears and accusations that the US is interfering in the election, and these follow similar allegations in a string of elections across Latin America which were won by Donald Trump-backed candidates in what is being called 'the orange wave'.

The Guardian's Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips, explains the tactics Trump and his administration have been using in recent months and what impact another Bolsonaro government could have on the region, and the world

Continue reading...
title: How Trump is meddling in Brazil's upcoming election – explainer

author: Nesrine Malik
description:
For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy.

When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on
title: Who’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone call

author: Alaina Demopoulos
description:
The US tried to forcibly assimilate the Lenape in brutal boarding schools, but a new exhibit proves their modern-day culture is vibrant and alive

During the 19th century, the US government funded more than 500 “Indian boarding schools” aimed at forcibly assimilating Native American children into western culture. Students were taken from their families, frequently by force, and forced to cut their hair. They were stripped of their original names, and taught to feel shame regarding their heritage and customs. Run like military academies, these institutions required children to wear uniforms and subjected them to severe physical punishment, such as solitary confinement and flogging. Richard Henry Pratt, who established the first of these schools, decl
title: Abducted, renamed, but still here – the art of the first Native New Yorkers and their fight for their land

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling author

The nation is crying out for a really enjoyable erotic mystery-thriller, a taste potentially at least as strong as the cosy-crime fetish currently dominating our every waking moment. The success of Paul Feig’s naughty-but-not-nice movie The Housemaid proves it. We are thirsting for a sexy encounter with a dishy yet maybe problematic nice-guy husband; we are pining for a damaged and dangerous beautiful wife; we are longing to identify with a vulnerable yet gutsy young person who finds herself in the middle of their creepy scenario and we are yearning to spend some time in a secluded luxury lakeside villa of gigantic modernist proportions down whose night-time corridors we can tremblingly tiptoe. So here is a drama, adapted by screenwriter Nick Antosca from the novel by Colleen Hoover, in which someone has such excitingly transgressi
title: Verity review – Dakota Johnson leaves teethmarks as she goes back to Fifty Shades erotic thriller territory

author: Mark Fisher
description:
Live theatre, Newcastle
Fictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debts

It sounds like a good plan. With credit cards maxed out, Colin Wilson will set off in his canoe and never come back. Once he is presumed dead, his wife, Deborah, will claim the life insurance. Pension and mortgage payouts will follow. Meanwhile, Colin will go into hiding until they can make a fresh start.

Inspired by the true story of “canoe man” John Darwin, Alison Carr’s two-hander looks as though it will head into the sitcom territory of Can You Keep a Secret? Like that BBC comedy, in which Mark Heap does a bad job at hiding, All at Sea considers the hurdles
title: All at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigue

author: Antonio Voce and Ashley Kirk
description:
These visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systems

New analysis produced exclusively for the Guardian reveals how different voting systems would return significantly different seat totals in the UK parliament, based on recent polling.

While the current first past the post (FPTP) system could leave Labour short of a majority with 250 seats, the modelling shows how proportional systems would be likely to reduce the number of seats given to the leading party – and give the UK a more finely balanced parliament that better represents the votes people cast.

Continue reading...
title: How could Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your area

author: Lucy Knight
description:
This shaggy beast is now plastered across everything from mugs to hot water bottles. Or you can sit on her, wrap yourself in her, wipe your feet on her …

Picture this: you get home from work, wipe your feet on your doormat, which has a picture of a highland cow on it, sniff the flowers growing from your highland cow-shaped plant pot, then step inside, hang your coat on one of your highland-cow-themed hooks and put some water on to boil in your highland cow kettle. When the tea is ready, you drink it from one of your highland cow mugs, plucked from a highland cow mug tree, discarding the teabag in a highland cow-emblazoned pedal bin. Oops, you’ve spilled a drop, but not to worry – there’s a fresh roll of kitchen roll waiting for you in between the resin cow-butt and cow-head of its highland cow-shaped holder.

You then carry the tea to your living room, and place it (atop a highland cow coaster, of course) on your coffee table, which has been carved into the shape
title: Udder madness: why are highland cows suddenly everywhere?

author: Sam Cunningham
description:
• Club have been found guilty of breaking financial rules

  • City deny wrongdoing, saying it is a ‘conspiracy theory’

Manchester City are set to owe the Premier League tens of millions of pounds in compensation for legal costs after being found guilty of virtually all charges brought against them.

The Premier League announced on Tuesday that an independent commission had determined the club had artificially inflated their income by £900m over a nine-year period. The panel concluded that Manchester City had arranged “sham” contracts to boost revenues to comply with spending rules.

Continue reading...
title: Manchester City could be forced to pay Premier League up to £50m in legal costs

author: Shrai Popat (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
description:
Lawmakers say ‘Congress must step in’ after supreme court ruled to allow Trump officials to resume deporting people where their lives could be in danger

  • US supreme court allows Trump officials to resume deportations to third countries

  • Sign up for the Breaking News US email

Donald Trump will be in Washington today. We’ll hear from him at 11am ET for a Hispanic Heritage month at the White House. Later, the president will make an announcement alongside the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, widely expected to be about a multibillion-dollar i
title: Democratic lawmakers call for protections over third country deportations after ‘indefensible’ court ruling – US politics live

author: Alim Kheraj
description:
Utilita Arena, Birmingham
First announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacle

The road to the Pussycat Dolls’ comeback tour has been fraught. Originally announced in 2019 with all but one of the group’s original members on board, the pandemic and then a legal dispute, led to its cancellation. After a few years of silence, three members – Nicole Scherzinger, Ashley Roberts and Kimberly Wyatt – shared plans for a 53-date world tour as a trio. Poor ticket sales nixed the US leg, though, while Maga-supporting former member Jessica Sutta alleged she was left out of the reunion because she was viewed as “a liability” (the group did not comment).

Does a girlband ostensibly created as a dance troupe work as a trio? While Scherzinger’s voice pushed them into pop stardom – they scored six UK Top 3 hits in their initial 2005-09 run – their appeal was large
title: The Pussycat Dolls review – Nicole Scherzinger’s star power dominates fraught reunion

author: Patrick Barkham
description:
The trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railway

The air is scented with the sweet tang of ladies bedstraw and made musical by skylark and blackcap song. An abundance of marbled white butterflies, small skippers and common blue damselflies dart over the flowering knapweed, yarrow and wild carrot.

That the largest chalk grassland in the Chilterns is full of wildlife may not surprise you. But the fact that it is completely artificial, only four years old and has been built by the much-maligned HS2, may do.

Continue reading...
title: Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 route

author: Tim Anderson, Maunika Gowardhan,. Mandy Yin, Keshia Sakarah
description:
A Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroom doria, an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthani papad ki sabji, and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplings

Curry runs through Malaysia’s veins; it’s in every kitchen and at every food stall, whether run by Malays, Chinese or Indians. We tend to cook curries using either a wet spice paste (rempah) straight from the morning market, or a good curry powder – every household keeps a pack of Adabi or Baba’s in the cupboard as a fallback; we have no shame in this at all. Only when you’ve got time on your hands, or you’re cooking to impress, do you build a rempah from scratch.

Continue reading...
title: From Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipes

author: Tom Hunt
description:
This sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanatics

While researching gherkins for a Food Filter column last year, I came across Kühne’s recipe for pickled cucumber ice-cream and couldn’t resist. Niche, I know, but I’ll bet there are a lot of gherkin fanatics out there who’d be willing to give it a go. If not, the cocktail I’ve used as inspiration might well suffice. The pickleback is made with pickle juice and a spirit such as whisky, tequila or, my favourite, vodka, and that same punchy, sweet-and-sour combination comes together to make possibly the quirkiest ice-cream flavour you ever come across. Delicious in a cone and topped with a gherkin, and out of this world when served wi
title: How to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipe | Waste not

author: Tom Service
description:
New York’s mayor Mamdani is putting his political capital behind one of our greatest art forms with his pledge of Opera for All – and 70,000 free tickets to prove it

Opera for All. It’s the credo of every opera house in the world, and each has its own ways and means of attracting new – and, crucially, younger – audiences. But it’s rare that one gives away thousands of tickets to anyone who applies. In New York last week, mayor Mamdani took to the stage of the Metropolitan Opera to tell his city that previously opera-shy citizens should apply for one of the 70,000 free tickets that he and the opera house are giving away this and every season. That means a staggering 10,000 free tickets a month. Not just for the under-25s, not just for the productions that they can’t shift tickets for on Mondays
title: Start spreading the news… New York’s opera giveaway shows UK politicians how to be brave

author: Gabrielle Canon in San Francisco
description:
Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska

Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.

The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.

Continue reading...
title: California rushes to prepare for massive ‘Kelvin’ wave and predicted sea level rise

author: The civil servant
description:
Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat

Another day, another apocalyptic warning about the likelihood that rampantly uncontrollable artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, including the problem of being alive.

Hot on the heels of disgruntled Anthropic researchers announcing the end of civilisation by 2030, we’ve now had the portentously named Hugging Face incident, as well as the Australian government’s grim discovery of a rogue AI’s attack on its Medicare website. Swarms of experts are now
title: Do you want help from humans or AI bots? Because the UK civil service is changing – and not for the better | The civil servant

author: Geoff Lemon (now) and Daniel Gallan (later)
description:
• Updates from the ODI match at NWC Oval

  • Start time in Potchefstroom is 1.30pm local/9.30pm AEST

  • Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email

Hello! Game 3 and final today, with South Africa already taking the series in the first two. It has been a battle of the middle overs, with the home spinners thoroughly doing the job over the visiting batting. Australia, defending champions, need a solution to getting tied down, with just a year to go until the next World Cup, also in South Africa. So, still a lot to play for today.

Continue reading...
title: South Africa v Australia: third men’s one-day international – live

author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
description:
PM has revealed more details about a proposed shake-up of adult social care – including a broad timetable

Andy Burnham’s Labour conference speech gave a little more detail on how he intends to take forward what he said at the start of his premiership would be his signature social policy ambition: an overhaul of adult social care.

This article was updated after official clarifications on future care policy plans were issued

title: How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?

author: Alexandra Villarreal
description:
After switching tactics, federal agents are detaining and deporting record numbers of people from the US

When federal agents fatally shot US citizen protesters Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January during the nation’s largest immigration-enforcement operation ever, it marked a turning point for the second Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

Donald Trump in his second term had sparked outrage and huge protests with federal immigration officers descending en masse to one Democratic-run city after another in what some leaders called militarized “invasions”. Los Angeles,
title: From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot

author: Isabel Brooks
description:
Work in the hospitality industry made me who I am. Without it, young people are denied not only an income and a step on the career ladder, but important life skills

Everyone remembers their first job. More often than not, it’s in the service industry. I started at 14, pouring drinks, serving food and standing with an ice-cream tray. This is where I learned how to handle mistakes, such as dropping an entire tray of prosecco glasses, or spraying hot coffee all over a bridesmaid because I plunged the cafetiere with too much gusto. I learned how to talk to angry strangers, and what it means to have a bad manager. I learned that the customer is always right, except when you’re talking to chefs, who will throw ham at your head if you tell them that. All in all, I did 10 years of restaurant, bar, pub and cafe work, from the age of 14 to 24, and I largely attribute the formation of my character to that decade of work.

But this kind of character-building experie
title: Prosecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiences | Isabel Brooks

author: Felicity Cloake
description:
An eclectic selection that will take you on a culinary journey – make room on your shelves

Kitchening by Jeremy Lee (4th Estate, £30)

Continue reading...
title: From cordon bleu to pasta and pies: the best autumn cookbooks for 2026 – reviewed

author: Adrian Horton
description:
In a new documentary, film-maker Erin Lee Carr lifts the lid on the 2000s TV show that shocked America

It was in 2003, while listening to country radio, that Kelly first heard the casting call: “Have you dreamed about plastic surgery but never thought you could afford it?” She immediately turned up the volume. The pitch sounded too good to be true: free cosmetic procedures, a nutritionist, self-esteem work – one “life-changing opportunity” that “could transform everything”. Kristy, Cindy, Tawnya and Beth heard the call, too: the chance to overhaul oneself from the outside in, fulfilling the implicit but omnipresent promise that if you just lost a little weight and just tweaked your face a bit, your whole life would open up. You, too, could be an ugly duckling transfigured into a swan.

The catch? It would all be filmed for television, of course, for a short-lived show that some have called one of the most sadistic of all time: The Swan. The Fox reality program, which ran
title: The Swan contestants on the most sadistic reality show on TV: ‘Ultimately, we were just a job’

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
National Gallery, London
Grab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes

‘They knew how to enjoy themselves,” David Hockney once told me, gleefully pointing out the cigarette and cigar butts littering the ground under Renoir’s dancers. There are broken clay-pipes too beneath the swirling pink skirts and blue trousers of the couple in his tall, narrow 1883 canvas Dance at Bougival as they bring their faces close, placing their arms around each other and pirouetting in the soft, airy space Renoir makes you feel as well as see. It’s an outdoor afternoon dance enclosed by fluffy, lime-coloured trees. A couple sitting at a table get friendlier with each swig of beer.

And oh, the lunches! Renoir seems to have invented the slow French lunch, relaxed and liquid, that launched a thousand bistro daydreams. In After the Luncheon, another one to delight Hoc
title: Renoir and Love review – ‘The happiest exhibition of the year! Et pourqoui pas?’

author: Damien Gayle
description:
Analysis has shown the costs of daily essentials soaring in recent years, thanks in part to climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensions

François Perrodo is what is known in motorsport as a gentleman driver. In June, he raced at Le Mans, earning a podium place. At the end of August he was back behind the wheel at the Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps. This time he won.

Gentleman drivers are wealthy individuals who fund their own participation. The FIA governing body caps costs to keep racing accessible to such enthusiasts. But for self-confessed petrolhead Perrodo, it is well within his means.

Continue reading...
title: Super-rich UK energy and food magnates’ wealth skyrockets amid global crises

author: Amandas Ong
description:
It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online

After a tiring day as a school maintenance worker, 28-year-old Paul loves nothing more than unwinding with a good romance novel – ideally one with a fantasy or horror element to it. He reads five or six a month – most recently Love Bytes, about an 8ft-tall werewolf woman who runs an extremely successful AI company and falls in love with a handsome ballroom instructor.

Paul got into romance fiction via what he calls its “more traditional” side – such as the Regency romance series Bridgerton. He is partially sighted, so he mostly reads on his Kindle, where he can adjust the font size. In the first Bridgerton novel, “Simon, the main character, has a speech impediment that he has to work through,” says Paul. “I’m more attached to that one. Typically, I don’t come across disabled protagonists that much.”
title: The secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’

author: Arif Hasan
description:
The quarterback is widely adored on and off the field. Whether he deserves the public spotlight is another question

Throughout the NFL’s history, we’ve had our fair share of clown princes. Not too long ago, Rob Gronkowski was the league’s court jester. That history extends back, through Pat McAfee and Chad Ochocinco, past Jared Allen and John Randle to Jim McMahon, Steve McMichael, John Riggins, Alex Karras and Billy “White Shoes” Johnson.

There’s probably something deeply insightful to say about the need for goofballs in a sport characterized by militarized order and a seriousness that borders on self-parody, but what’s important now is how we reflect on these chosen merrymakers.

Continue reading...
title: Jameis Winston is now the New York Giants’ starter. He’s far from a goofball hero though

author: Sukhdev Sandhu
description:
The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works

Dèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online screeds about how “our country is under attack”, obsessed by cane toads who’ve been coming in from the Amazon basin. As she scrambles to the floor of a restaurant called Oasis, surrounded by dozens of diners playing dead, a man asks, “Is this a mass grave?”

Things have always been tough for Magnolia. Her mother chases pigeons by day, sleepwalks at night, is on and off lithium. Her father worked for many years as a bus driver in Brooklyn, saving every cent so he could buy a nice retirement home back in Haiti. She was brought up by an “aunt” whose family had been kill
title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in Miami

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Pedro Almodóvar provides a vocal cameo and his style can be traced back to this influential film

This cult supernatural mystery from 1979 is a deeply strange cheese dream of a film from Spain, in which almost the entire opening 10 minutes unfolds in a jittery quiet. There are some longueurs and some pop-eyed silent-movie acting from one of its leads, yes, but also a deeply unnerving, enveloping atmosphere of dread.

At least some of its fascination stems from the marginal involvement of the young Pedro Almodóvar, who did voice-overdubbing for one female character. Director Iván Zulueta was to maintain his connection with Almodóvar from then on and much of Almodóvar’s procedure can be traced back to this influential film: the rapture for movies (what a character here calls “cinemania”), the double-stranded narrative, the queer euphoria and the importance of extended flashbacks.
title: Rapture review – cult Spanish horror is a deeply strange cheese dream of cinemania

author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
description:
Co-founder of independent website Tapajós de Fato said decision was made to protect journalists and their families

Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon.

Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next.

Continue reading...
title: ‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats

author: Rachel Dixon
description:
Converted from Victorian buffet bars, ticket offices and waiting rooms, these station pubs offer beautifully restored interiors, real ales and a slice of railway history

No prizes for guessing what this pub used to be… The Old Ticket Office has high ceilings, walls painted shades of locomotive green and booths resembling train carriages; there are outdoor tables on Station Square. A live train departures board theoretically prevents passengers lingering too long, and a canning machine means any draught beer is also available to take away (the hatch on platform 4 also does takeaway orders). There are five handpulls plus Young’s usual spritz menu and other drinks, plus light bites and pizzas. The pub is currently closed for roof repairs and expected to reopen by the end of October.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Delays are always welcome’: 10 of the best railway station pubs in the UK

author: Phil Harrison, Priya Elan, Jack Seale and Graeme Virtue
description:
Richard Armitage’s smug scientist and Annabel Scholey’s frosty cop team up to solve a murder. Plus Martin Compston’s raucous cocktail sesh in Las Vegas. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, ITV1
If you have room for one more mismatched detective duo in your life, this new drama introduces Dr Ethan Winter (Richard Armitage), an unbearably smug forensic pathologist who can “read a body like a book”, and DI Lauren Bell (Annabel Scholey), a diligent, frosty cop. The pair are on a collision course as the murder of a young woman lands in their in trays. But when an explosive postmortem raises the stakes, they are forced to tolerate each other. Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: a new mismatched detective duo for crime drama fans

author: Lisa O’Carroll, senior correspondent
description:
The PM said Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’ and wants an assessment before the next UK-EU summit

Andy Burnham has said Brexit has “done more harm than good” and pledged to launch a major review of the UK’s relationship with the EU, opening the door to a potential referendum over rejoining the union.

He said he would “lay out options” around the time of the next EU-UK summit, due to be held at the end of November or soon after.

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI

Poor Greta Garbo.

Perhaps, in life, she thought her final indignity would be the Peter Cook and Dudley Moore TV sketch from 1970, showing Pete as the legendary recluse standing on the back of a flatbed truck as it rumbles through the crowded city streets, shouting at everyone through a megaphone: “I vant to be alone!”

Continue reading...
title: SKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the future

author: Patrick Barkham
description:
More species are squeezing in an extra generation before colder weather arrives

Summer is over, most flowers were frazzled long ago and we might expect to see few butterflies beyond September. But it is not over yet.

The reverberations from one of the best butterfly seasons in Britain this century will continue if there is more autumn sunshine.

Continue reading...
title: Autumn sunshine could extend Britain’s bumper year for butterflies

author: Ali Stoner
description:
Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples

There is a depth and history to Scotland’s food that reaches far beyond deep-fried Mars bars or urban myths about haggis. Kitchens were humble and full of life – recipes passed by word of mouth, scraps of paper shared between friends, generations stitching together simple meals. I’m lucky enough that my mum taught me how a potato, a handful of oatmeal and a bit of salt and butter could make a meal and hold a story, but life changes – new ingredients arrive, we move away, time grows shorter – and, sometimes, those simple, comforting recipes drift out of reach. Today’s dishes began as a keepsake for my children – to save old recipes, to record a feeling of home – but also as an invitation to discover what happens when memory meets invention.
title: Cullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classics

author: Alexandra Pearce-Broomhead
description:
Camborne, Cornwall: There will be more storms like Goretti and more fires next summer, but we can make the landscape more resilient

A grey wagtail flits at the stream’s edge, its flaxen underbelly matching the woodland’s autumn swatch. A few months ago, this bird may have struggled to catch a midge or water snail here, after the streambed nearly ran dry. Sitting by the water now, it’s easy to forget the damage this area suffered this year. But the land remembers.

Many months on from Storm Goretti, the entrance to these woods is still a battlefield of fallen trees, Scots pines and ageing oaks torn ungainly from the ground. Just over a mile away, a gorse break is still scarred from a late-summer wildfire that blackened the coastline. I stopped by the other day; the western gorse should have been blooming, delicate coconut notes luring in late
title: Country diary: The land here is scarred from a year of hard weather – now what will winter hold? | Alexandra Pearce-Broomhead

author: Jigyasa Mishra, Nuwakot district
description:
Kalpana Nepali was seven months pregnant when the catastrophic flash floods hit last month, while Pooja Pariyal spent three days on a hospital roof waiting to be rescued. Now, they are living precariously in temporary shelters

For three days, Pooja Pariyal waited on the roof of Trishuli hospital with her three-month-old daughter, Ridhika. On the ground below and around the building, most of her town had been destroyed and churned into a sea of mud in the catastrophic flash floods that surged through the Himayalan border region of Nepal and Tibet in August.

“Those three days were living hell for me, with no food, no working toilet and no one to help with the baby,” she says. “I had nothing to clean my baby’s soiled clothes. My milk supply had reduced because I was hungry and this poor little thing would cry her lungs out
title: ‘I do not know if the doctor survived’: young mothers recall ‘living hell’ of Nepal’s floods

author: María Ramírez
description:
Pédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homes

Maricarmen Abascal is a determined woman who uses a wheelchair to get around. She has needed her determination over the years she has spent fighting the real estate company that forced her out of her Madrid apartment last week. She had lived in the flat for more than 70 of her 87 years.

Police forced their way into her apartment after a judge approved Abascal’s eviction. By then, protesters had gathered around the building, including the actor Carlos Bardem, Javier’s brother. Teargas was used against them. Abascal was taken to a Madrid hospital, suffering from anxiety and extreme
title: It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María Ramírez

author: Interviews by Miriam Gillinson
description:
The musical powerhouse has spawned huge hits, but which do its troupers love to belt out – even for the 1,700th time? From Broadway legend Idina Menzel to composer Stephen Schwartz, they reveal all

Idina Menzel originated the role of Elphaba, the witch of the west who turns out not to be so wicked (but still very green). She won a Tony on Broadway, starred in the West End run and made a cheeky cameo in the recent film version

Continue reading...
title: ‘They’ll never bring us dowwwwwwwn!’ Wicked’s stars pick their favourite songs from the smash hit

author: Chris Godfrey
description:
Six months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countryside

Samba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the dense Hampshire countryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive.

Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says
title: ‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybara

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Comments come after Moscow warned it would ‘deploy its entire arsenal’ if Kaliningrad was threatened. What we know on day 1,680

Continue reading...
title: Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify

author: Eva Corlett in Wellington and Kat Wong in Sydney
description:
More than 100,000 have enrolled to vote from abroad in the November poll, and many are unhappy with how things look back home

New Zealander Kris Taute has lived in Australia for 15 years, but his head and heart are turning towards his home country and a looming general election that could be influenced by a large block of overseas voters.

From across the Tasman Sea, Taute has felt growing frustration at New Zealand’s centre-right coalition government, and analysts believe large numbers of New Zealanders who have left the country since they came to power in 2023 may be poised to vent their grievances at the ballot box in November.

Continue reading...
title: A tight election looms in New Zealand. This time, overseas voters could be bad news for the big parties

author: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent
description:
Coverage levels fall a million square kilometres short of the long-term average, with global heating likely driving losses

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling a million square kilometres – or almost 400,000 square miles – short of the long-term average, scientists have confirmed.

Confirmation of the peak meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and crit
title: Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’
